newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO, Bildt condemn attack on Bosnian Moslems.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Bildt condemn attack on Bosnian Moslems.

text.p: NATO and international officials condemned Bosnian Serb authorities on Monday for allowing a Serb mob to attack Moslems preparing housing for the resettlement of a village in Serb-controlled territory.

At least three Moslems were injured on Sunday by a mob as they tried to begin construction of temporary housing in the village of Gajevi near the ethnic boundary line between Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
Major Tony White, a spokesman for the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR), said the U.S. commander of SFOR blamed Serb authorities for allowing the attacks to take place.
"General (William) Crouch is outraged ...and strongly condemns the relevant (Serb) authorities for allowing this despicable act to take place," White told reporters.

The SFOR commander was disturbed that Serb civilians were "clearly organised with a violent intent" to prevent refugees from returning to their pre-war homes and that Serb police had shown "obvious and blatant inaction", White said.
The office for the international High Representative to Bosnia also slammed Serb authorities for the attack.
"What took place yesterday was obviously a clear violation of the Dayton peace agreement, its humanitarian annex specifically," said Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the High Representative.

General Crouch, the international High Representative to Bosnia Carl Bildt and the head of U.N. police monitors Peter Fitzgerald met Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic later on Monday to convey their dismay.

Plavsic's office issued a statement afterward condemning "any form of violence and failure to observe the procedure for the return of refugees which results in incidents in the separation zones, irrespective of which side causes them," the Serb news agency SRNA reported.
The Bosnian Serb interior ministry had been ordered to carry out an investigation and establish who was responsible for the attacks, it said.

A group of 36 Moslem families is scheduled to return to Gajevi after submitting to a vetting procedure by international agencies devised to confirm they are former residents of the northeast Bosnian village.
Some of the Moslem workers who were attacked accused U.S. and Russian peacekeeping troops patrolling the area of failing to intervene to halt the Serb mob.
As U.S. combat helicopters circled overhead, about 200 Serbs descended on the Moslem workers twice on Sunday, punching them and using wooden planks from the construction site as clubs.
The Serbs tore down walls of prefabricated houses and tried to torch one of the homes as well, SFOR said in a statement issued from a U.S. base in Tuzla.
SFOR said it was up to local police and not the NATO-led force to maintain law and order and to handle civil disturbances. "SFOR is not a police force," it said.
